public_rationale: The record supports concern about limited dedicated oversight: NIST's contemporary framework was voluntary. But existing legal authority and Italy's action against Replika prevent treating chatbots as operating in a demonstrated legal vacuum. Neither a voluntary framework nor an isolated enforcement action settles how extensive regulation was. The retrieved evidence does not establish the broad claim under a single, well-supported jurisdictional reading.
limitations: Several relevant contemporary primary pages could not be read.
Later legal summaries are context, not date-matched outcome evidence.
The speaker did not define jurisdiction or regulatory scope.

public_payload.normalized_proposition: There is almost no regulation of AI chatbots.

statement.excerpt: There are almost no regulations here; we are living in the Wild AI West.

our_interpretation: The ordinary reading is that binding oversight of consumer AI chatbots was sparse, especially concerning deployment and harmful or unreliable responses.
The claim does not expressly exclude generally applicable consumer-protection and privacy laws.
I examine the United States as the main contextual reading, while flagging that Marcus did not specify a jurisdiction.
The target is the legal position on the publication date. Legal requirements do not have a quarterly reporting period.
Almost no permits some exceptions; finding one applicable law would not alone refute it.
criteria.support_condition: A sufficiently complete account of applicable law shows that chatbot deployment and the behavior discussed faced very few substantive, binding requirements.
criteria.contradiction_condition: Applicable laws imposed substantial, enforceable requirements across the relevant deployment practices and chatbot harms, making near-absence of regulation an inaccurate description.
